title: Energy: KE, GPE and Power
description: Calculate kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, work done and power — all recall equations you must memorise.

method_card.title: Energy: KE, GPE and Power
method_card.content:
This lesson covers five recall equations — none of them are on the equation sheet, so you need to know them from memory.

Approach for every calculation:

  1. Read the question — what are you asked to find?
  2. Identify the correct equation from memory
  3. List the values you're given and convert units if needed
  4. Substitute into the equation and calculate
  5. Write your answer with the correct unit

Common pitfalls:

  • Speed is squared in the KE equation — doubling speed quadruples KE
  • Convert time to seconds before using the power equation
  • Convert mass to kg (not grams) and speed to m/s
  • Use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg unless told otherwise
  • 1 kJ = 1000 J, 1 kW = 1000 W, 1 MW = 1,000,000 W
steps: Read the question — what quantity are you finding? (energy, power, speed, height?)
Recall the correct equation from memory
Convert all units (g→kg, mins→s, km/h→m/s, kJ→J)
Substitute values and calculate
State your answer with the correct unit (J, W, kJ, kW)

exam_context.frequency: Every exam — energy calculations appear on every Paper 1

worked_examples.question: A ball of mass 0.4 kg is thrown at a speed of 10 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
A crane lifts a 250 kg beam to a height of 12 m in 30 seconds. Calculate the power of the crane. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A roller coaster car of mass 500 kg is at the top of a 40 m hill. Calculate its speed at the bottom, assuming all GPE converts to KE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.label: Step 1 — Calculate GPE at the top
Step 2 — Set GPE = KE and rearrange for v

bronze.display: A car has a mass of 1200 kg and travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: 15² = 225. Then KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J.
Don't forget the ½. KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J, not 270,000 J.

bronze.display: A 0.5 kg ball is held 4 m above the ground. Calculate its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A force of 50 N pushes a box 8 m along the floor. Calculate the work done.

misconceptions.message: Work done = force × distance = 50 × 8 = 400 J.

bronze.display: A kettle transfers 180,000 J of energy in 3 minutes. Calculate its power in watts.

misconceptions.message: Convert minutes to seconds first: 3 min = 180 s. P = 180,000 ÷ 180 = 1000 W.

bronze.display: A runner of mass 60 kg sprints at 8 m/s. Calculate their kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed: 8² = 64. KE = ½ × 60 × 64 = 1920 J.

bronze.display: A bag of mass 3 kg is lifted onto a shelf 2.5 m high. Calculate the GPE gained. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A motor does 5000 J of work in 20 seconds. Calculate its power.

misconceptions.message: Power = energy ÷ time = 5000 ÷ 20 = 250 W. Don't multiply.

bronze.display: Which equation would you use to calculate the energy stored by an object lifted above the ground?

misconceptions.message: An object above the ground has gravitational PE. Use Eₚ = mgh. KE is for moving objects.

silver.display: A cyclist and bike have a combined mass of 80 kg and travel at 12 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: 12² = 144. Then ½ × 80 × 144 = 5760 J = 5.76 kJ.

silver.display: A 60 W light bulb is left on for 2 hours. Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Convert hours to seconds: 2 h = 7200 s. E = Pt = 60 × 7200 = 432,000 J = 432 kJ.

silver.display: A crane lifts a 400 kg load to a height of 15 m. Calculate the work done by the crane. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: First find the weight: W = mg = 400 × 9.8 = 3920 N. Then work done = Fs = 3920 × 15 = 58,800 J.

silver.display: A car of mass 900 kg accelerates from rest to 30 m/s. Calculate the work done on the car.

misconceptions.message: Work done = change in KE = ½ × 900 × 30² = ½ × 900 × 900 = 405,000 J.
Don't forget to square the speed: 30² = 900. KE = ½ × 900 × 900 = 405,000 J.

silver.display: A 1500 W motor lifts a 50 kg mass. How high can it lift the mass in 10 seconds? Give your answer to 1 d.p. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A 200 g tennis ball is served at 50 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

misconceptions.message: Convert grams to kg: 200 g = 0.2 kg. KE = ½ × 0.2 × 50² = ½ × 0.2 × 2500 = 250 J.

gold.display: A skydiver of mass 75 kg falls from 4000 m to 3000 m. Calculate the speed they would reach if all the lost GPE converted to KE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Use the height difference (4000 − 3000 = 1000 m), not the total height.

gold.display: A car of mass 1100 kg travels at 20 m/s. The driver brakes, and the car decelerates to 8 m/s. Calculate the work done by the brakes.
An electric motor has a power rating of 2.5 kW. It lifts a 80 kg object 6 m in 4 seconds. Calculate the efficiency of the motor. Give your answer as a percentage. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Useful output = mgh = 80 × 9.8 × 6 = 4704 J. Total input = Pt = 2500 × 4 = 10,000 J. Efficiency = 4704/10,000 × 100 = 47.04%.
Convert kW to W: 2.5 kW = 2500 W. Then total input energy = 2500 × 4 = 10,000 J.

gold.display: Two students climb the same flight of stairs (height 4 m). Student A has mass 50 kg and takes 5 seconds. Student B has mass 70 kg and takes 8 seconds. Which student has greater power output? Enter A or B.

misconceptions.message: Power A = mgh/t = (50 × 9.8 × 4)/5 = 392 W. Power B = (70 × 9.8 × 4)/8 = 343 W. Student A has greater power.

gold.display: A ball of mass 0.3 kg is dropped from a height of 10 m. It bounces back to a height of 6 m. Calculate the energy dissipated during the bounce. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: GPE before = 0.3 × 9.8 × 10 = 29.4 J. GPE after = 0.3 × 9.8 × 6 = 17.64 J. Energy dissipated = 29.4 − 17.64 = 11.76 J.

gold.display: A wind turbine generates 1.5 MW of power. How much energy does it transfer in one day? Give your answer in standard form.

title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
description: Calculate efficiency from energy and power values, find useful and wasted energy, and interpret Sankey diagrams.

method_card.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
method_card.content:
Efficiency tells you how good a device is at converting energy into the form you want. It's a recall equation — not on the equation sheet.

Key strategy:

  1. Identify the useful output energy (or power) — this is the form you actually want
  2. Identify the total input energy (or power) — everything that goes in
  3. Divide useful by total to get efficiency as a decimal
  4. Multiply by 100 if the question asks for a percentage

Critical rules:

  • Efficiency can never exceed 1 (or 100%) — if your answer is above this, you've divided the wrong way round
  • Wasted energy = total input − useful output
  • You can use either energy values or power values — never mix them
  • On Sankey diagrams, the width of each arrow is proportional to the energy — read the scale carefully

Common exam pitfall: Questions sometimes give you wasted energy instead of useful energy. Always check which one you've been given before dividing.
steps: Identify the useful output and the total input (energy or power)
Check you're not accidentally using wasted energy as the useful output
Divide: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input
Multiply by 100 if the question asks for a percentage
Check your answer is less than 1 (or 100%) — if not, you've divided the wrong way

exam_context.frequency: Very common — efficiency appears in almost every Paper 1

worked_examples.question: A light bulb receives 100 J of electrical energy and converts 10 J to light. Calculate the efficiency of the bulb.
A motor has an input power of 500 W and wastes 175 W as heat and sound. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find the useful power output

worked_examples.question: An electric motor with an efficiency of 0.80 is used to lift a 50 kg crate to a height of 3 m. Calculate the total electrical energy input to the motor. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.label: Step 1 — Calculate the useful output (GPE gained)

bronze.display: A heater receives 2000 J of electrical energy and converts 1600 J to heat for the room. Calculate the efficiency of the heater.

misconceptions.message: Divide useful by total, not total by useful. Efficiency = 1600 ÷ 2000 = 0.8.
Useful output (1600 J) is the heat for the room. Efficiency = 1600/2000 = 0.8.

bronze.display: A motor has an input energy of 500 J and a useful output of 350 J. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = 350/500 = 0.7. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage: 0.7 × 100 = 70%.

bronze.display: An LED bulb has an input power of 10 W and a useful light output of 7 W. Calculate the efficiency.

misconceptions.message: You can use power values directly. Efficiency = useful power ÷ total power = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7.

bronze.display: A car engine receives 40,000 J of chemical energy from fuel and converts 12,000 J to kinetic energy. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 12,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.3 = 30%. Don't divide 40,000 by 12,000.

bronze.display: A kettle is 90% efficient. It receives 200,000 J of electrical energy. Calculate the useful heat energy transferred to the water.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.9 × 200,000 = 180,000 J. Convert 90% to 0.9 first.

bronze.display: A power station has an efficiency of 0.35. The total input power is 800 MW. Calculate the useful electrical power output in MW.

misconceptions.message: Useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.35 × 800 = 280 MW.
Both values are already in MW, so the answer stays in MW. No conversion needed.

bronze.display: A Sankey diagram shows a light bulb receiving 80 J of electrical energy. The useful light output arrow has a width of 8 J. Calculate the wasted energy.

misconceptions.message: Wasted energy = total input − useful output = 80 − 8 = 72 J. Energy is conserved.

bronze.display: Which of these devices is the most efficient?
options: Device A: 500 J in, 200 J useful out
Device B: 400 J in, 300 J useful out
Device C: 1000 J in, 600 J useful out
Device D: 200 J in, 50 J useful out

misconceptions.message: Calculate each: A = 200/500 = 0.40, B = 300/400 = 0.75, C = 600/1000 = 0.60, D = 50/200 = 0.25. Device B is the most efficient at 75%.

silver.display: A motor receives 5000 J of electrical energy. It wastes 1500 J as heat and 500 J as sound. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

misconceptions.message: Useful = total − all wasted = 5000 − 1500 − 500 = 3000 J. Efficiency = 3000/5000 = 0.6 = 60%.
Remember to subtract ALL the wasted energies (heat and sound) from the input.

silver.display: A wind turbine has an efficiency of 0.40. In one hour it generates 720 kJ of useful electrical energy. Calculate the total energy input from the wind in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ.
Don't multiply: total input = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ. The total must be MORE than the useful output.

silver.display: A gas boiler is 92% efficient and provides 46,000 J of useful heat energy. Calculate the total energy wasted by the boiler.

misconceptions.message: First find total input: 46,000 ÷ 0.92 = 50,000 J. Then wasted = total − useful = 50,000 − 46,000 = 4000 J.

silver.display: A hydroelectric power station converts the GPE of falling water into electricity. 8000 kg of water falls through 50 m every second. The station has an efficiency of 0.85. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: GPE per second = mgh = 8000 × 9.8 × 50 = 3,920,000 W. Useful output = efficiency × input power = 0.85 × 3,920,000 = 3,332,000 W.
Since the water falls every second, mgh gives energy per second — which is power in watts.

silver.display: An electric drill has a power rating of 750 W and an efficiency of 0.60. Calculate the power wasted as heat and sound.

misconceptions.message: Useful = efficiency × total = 0.60 × 750 = 450 W. Wasted = 750 − 450 = 300 W.
Find useful power first (efficiency × input), then subtract from total to get wasted power.

silver.display: A Sankey diagram for a coal power station shows 1000 MJ input. The useful electricity arrow is 350 MJ and the cooling tower waste arrow is 500 MJ. Calculate the energy lost through other waste pathways.

misconceptions.message: Total in = all out. Other waste = 1000 − 350 − 500 = 150 MJ. Energy is always conserved.

gold.display: A crane motor with an efficiency of 0.75 lifts a 120 kg steel beam to a height of 20 m. Calculate the total electrical energy input to the motor. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Useful output = GPE = mgh = 120 × 9.8 × 20 = 23,520 J. Total input = useful ÷ efficiency = 23,520 ÷ 0.75 = 31,360 J.
Don't multiply useful by efficiency. Total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 25 m/s. The engine has an efficiency of 0.30. Calculate the total chemical energy released from the fuel.

misconceptions.message: First find KE gained: ½ × 1200 × 25² = ½ × 1200 × 625 = 375,000 J. This is the useful output. Total input = 375,000 ÷ 0.30 = 1,250,000 J.
Remember to square the speed: 25² = 625, not 25 × 2 = 50.

gold.display: A solar panel converts sunlight into 240 W of useful electrical power. The panel is 20% efficient. The Sun delivers 800 W/m² to the panel. Calculate the area of the panel.

misconceptions.message: Total input power = useful ÷ efficiency = 240 ÷ 0.20 = 1200 W. Area = total power ÷ power per m² = 1200 ÷ 800 = 1.5 m².
First find total power input, then divide by the solar intensity to find the area.

gold.display: A pump with a power rating of 600 W and an efficiency of 0.70 lifts water to a height of 8 m for 5 minutes. Calculate the mass of water lifted. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Remember to account for the efficiency — only 70% of the input energy lifts the water.

gold.display: A student compares two kettles. Kettle A is 88% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 2000 W. Kettle B is 95% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 1800 W. Which kettle transfers more useful energy to the water? Enter A or B.

misconceptions.message: Kettle A: useful = 0.88 × 2000 × 180 = 316,800 J. Kettle B: useful = 0.95 × 1800 × 180 = 307,800 J. Despite B being more efficient, A transfers more useful energy because of its higher power rating.

gold.display: Which statement about efficiency is correct?
options: A more powerful device is always more efficient
Efficiency can be greater than 100% if the device is very good
Wasted energy is eventually transferred to the surroundings, increasing the temperature
Renewable energy sources always have higher efficiency than fossil fuels

misconceptions.message: Efficiency can never exceed 100% (conservation of energy). Power and efficiency are different things. Wasted energy always ends up heating the surroundings — this is correct.

title: Circuit Calculations
description: Use V = IR and Q = It for series and parallel circuits, calculate total resistance, and find current and voltage in branches.

method_card.title: Circuit Calculations
method_card.content:
Circuit calculations use two core recall equations plus rules for combining resistors.

Key strategy:

  1. Identify whether the circuit is series or parallel
  2. In series — current is the same everywhere, voltages add up, resistances add up
  3. In parallel — voltage is the same across each branch, currents add up, and total resistance decreases
  4. Find the total resistance first, then use Ohm's law to find current or voltage

Common pitfalls:

  • In parallel circuits, the total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistor — if your answer is bigger, you've added instead of using the reciprocal method
  • Time must be in seconds for the charge equation
  • Check whether the question asks for current through the whole circuit or through one branch
  • In series, the battery voltage is shared between components; in parallel, each branch gets the full battery voltage
steps: Identify: is the circuit series or parallel?
Calculate total resistance (add for series; reciprocal method for parallel)
Use V = IR to find the unknown (rearrange as needed: I = V/R or R = V/I)
For charge questions, use Q = It (with time in seconds)
Check your answer — does the current direction and size make sense?

exam_context.frequency: Every exam — circuit calculations appear on every Paper 1

worked_examples.question: A resistor has a resistance of 20 Ω. The current through it is 0.5 A. Calculate the voltage across the resistor.
Two resistors of 6 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the total resistance of the combination.

steps.label: Step 2 — Find a common denominator and add

worked_examples.question: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor in series with two parallel resistors of 6 Ω each. Calculate the current drawn from the battery.

bronze.display: A 12 V battery is connected to a 6 Ω resistor. Calculate the current flowing through the resistor.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange V = IR to I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A. Don't multiply V × R.
Current = voltage ÷ resistance = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A.

bronze.display: A current of 3 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. Calculate the voltage across it.

misconceptions.message: V = IR = 3 × 10 = 30 V. No rearranging needed here — just multiply.

bronze.display: A current of 0.5 A flows for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows.

misconceptions.message: Convert minutes to seconds: 2 min = 120 s. Q = It = 0.5 × 120 = 60 C.

bronze.display: Three resistors of 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance.

misconceptions.message: In series, just add: R = 4 + 6 + 10 = 20 Ω. Don't use the parallel (reciprocal) method.

bronze.display: A lamp has a voltage of 6 V across it and a current of 0.25 A through it. Calculate its resistance.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange V = IR to R = V/I = 6/0.25 = 24 Ω.
R = V ÷ I = 6 ÷ 0.25 = 24 Ω. Don't do I ÷ V.

bronze.display: A charge of 450 C passes through a wire in 5 minutes. Calculate the current.

misconceptions.message: Convert minutes to seconds: 5 min = 300 s. Rearrange: I = Q/t = 450/300 = 1.5 A.

bronze.display: Which equation links voltage, current and resistance?

misconceptions.message: V = IR is Ohm's law — it links voltage, current and resistance. P = VI is electrical power. Q = It is charge flow.

bronze.display: A 9 V battery drives a current of 0.3 A through a circuit for 40 seconds. Calculate the total charge that flows.

misconceptions.message: Q = It = 0.3 × 40 = 12 C. The voltage is not needed for this calculation.

silver.display: Two resistors of 10 Ω and 15 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the total resistance of the combination.

misconceptions.message: In parallel: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6. So R = 6 Ω. Don't just add them (that's series).
After finding 1/R = 1/6, you must flip it to get R = 6 Ω. Don't leave your answer as 1/6.

silver.display: A series circuit has a 12 V battery and two resistors: 8 Ω and 16 Ω. Calculate the voltage across the 16 Ω resistor.

misconceptions.message: Total R = 8 + 16 = 24 Ω. Current = V/R = 12/24 = 0.5 A. Voltage across 16 Ω = IR = 0.5 × 16 = 8 V.
You can't just use 12 V — the voltage is shared. Find the current first, then use V = IR for the 16 Ω resistor.

silver.display: A parallel circuit has a 6 V battery connected to two branches. Branch 1 has a 12 Ω resistor and branch 2 has a 4 Ω resistor. Calculate the total current drawn from the battery.

misconceptions.message: In parallel, each branch gets the full 6 V. I₁ = 6/12 = 0.5 A. I₂ = 6/4 = 1.5 A. Total I = 0.5 + 1.5 = 2 A.
Don't add the resistances (that's series). In parallel, find each branch current separately and add them.

silver.display: Three identical resistors of 12 Ω are connected in parallel. Calculate the total resistance.

misconceptions.message: 1/R = 1/12 + 1/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4. So R = 4 Ω. For n identical resistors in parallel, R_total = R/n.

silver.display: A current of 250 mA flows through a 1.2 kΩ resistor. Calculate the voltage across it.

misconceptions.message: You must convert mA to A (÷ 1000) and kΩ to Ω (× 1000) before substituting.

silver.display: A battery pushes 180 C of charge through a lamp in 3 minutes. Calculate the current through the lamp.

misconceptions.message: Convert time: 3 min = 180 s. I = Q/t = 180/180 = 1 A.

gold.display: A 24 V battery is connected to a 10 Ω resistor in series with two parallel resistors of 8 Ω and 24 Ω. Calculate the current drawn from the battery.

misconceptions.message: Parallel combination: 1/R = 1/8 + 1/24 = 3/24 + 1/24 = 4/24 = 1/6, so R_parallel = 6 Ω. Total R = 10 + 6 = 16 Ω. I = V/R = 24/16 = 1.5 A.
Don't add all three resistors. The 8 Ω and 24 Ω are in parallel (use reciprocal method), then add the result to the 10 Ω.

gold.display: A 24 V battery is connected to a 10 Ω resistor in series with two parallel resistors of 8 Ω and 24 Ω. Calculate the voltage across the parallel combination.

misconceptions.message: Parallel: 1/R = 1/8 + 1/24 = 4/24 = 1/6, R = 6 Ω. Total R = 10 + 6 = 16 Ω. Current = 24/16 = 1.5 A. Voltage across parallel pair = IR = 1.5 × 6 = 9 V. (Or: 24 − V across 10 Ω = 24 − 15 = 9 V.)
You need to find the total current first, then use V = IR for the parallel section (using its combined resistance of 6 Ω).

gold.display: A 6 V battery is connected to a 3 Ω resistor. Calculate the power dissipated by the resistor using \(P = I^2R\).

misconceptions.message: First find I = V/R = 6/3 = 2 A. Then P = I²R = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12 W.
Remember to square the current: I² = 2² = 4, not 2. P = 4 × 3 = 12 W.

gold.display: A filament lamp is labelled '12 V, 36 W'. Calculate its resistance when operating at its rated power.

misconceptions.message: From P = VI: I = P/V = 36/12 = 3 A. Then R = V/I = 12/3 = 4 Ω. Or use P = V²/R, so R = V²/P = 144/36 = 4 Ω.
You need to combine two equations. Find current first (I = P/V) then use R = V/I.

gold.display: Two resistors are connected in series to a 10 V battery. The current is 0.4 A and one resistor is 15 Ω. Calculate the resistance of the second resistor.

misconceptions.message: Total R = V/I = 10/0.4 = 25 Ω. Second resistor = 25 − 15 = 10 Ω.
Find total resistance first using Ohm's law, then subtract the known resistor.

gold.display: A circuit contains a 9 V battery, a switch and a 45 Ω resistor. The switch is closed for 10 minutes. Calculate the total charge that flows through the circuit.

misconceptions.message: First find I = V/R = 9/45 = 0.2 A. Convert time: 10 min = 600 s. Then Q = It = 0.2 × 600 = 120 C.
Convert 10 minutes to 600 seconds before using Q = It.

title: Electrical Power and Energy Bills
description: Calculate electrical power, energy transferred, energy in kilowatt-hours and the cost of electricity usage.

method_card.title: Electrical Power and Energy Bills
method_card.content:
This lesson covers four recall equations for electrical power and energy, plus the domestic energy billing method using kilowatt-hours.

Choosing the right equation:

  • Know voltage and current? Use the power equation with both
  • Know current and resistance? Use the alternative power equation
  • Know power and time? Use the energy equation
  • Know charge and voltage? Use the charge-based energy equation

Energy bills strategy:

  1. Convert power to kilowatts (÷ 1000)
  2. Convert time to hours
  3. Multiply to get energy in kWh (kilowatt-hours) — this is the 'unit' on your bill
  4. Multiply kWh by the price per unit to get the cost

Common pitfalls:

  • Don't mix up joules and kilowatt-hours — they're both energy but different units
  • For fuse calculations, find current using the power equation then choose the next fuse size up
  • 1 kWh is NOT 1000 J — it's the energy used by a 1 kW device in 1 hour = 3,600,000 J
steps: Identify what you're given and what you need to find
Choose the right equation based on the values you have
For energy bills: convert to kW and hours first, then multiply for kWh
For cost: multiply kWh by price per unit
For fuse ratings: calculate the current and pick the next standard fuse size up

exam_context.frequency: Very common — energy bills and power questions appear regularly on Paper 1

worked_examples.question: A toaster draws a current of 4 A from a 230 V mains supply. Calculate its power.
A 2.5 kW oven is used for 1.5 hours. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. Calculate the cost of running the oven.
A hairdryer has a power rating of 2000 W and operates on a 230 V supply. Available fuse ratings are 3 A, 5 A and 13 A. Which fuse should be used?

steps.label: Step 3 — Choose the fuse
steps.content: The current is 8.70 A. The fuse must be the next size above the normal operating current.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: 13 A fuse (the 5 A would blow under normal use)

bronze.display: A lamp draws a current of 0.5 A from a 12 V battery. Calculate the power of the lamp.

misconceptions.message: P = VI = 12 × 0.5 = 6 W. Just multiply voltage by current.

bronze.display: A 100 W light bulb is on for 60 seconds. Calculate the energy transferred.

misconceptions.message: E = Pt = 100 × 60 = 6000 J. Time is already in seconds.

bronze.display: A current of 2 A flows through a 5 Ω resistor. Calculate the power dissipated.

misconceptions.message: Square the current first: I² = 2² = 4. Then P = I²R = 4 × 5 = 20 W.
When you have current and resistance, use P = I²R. P = 4 × 5 = 20 W.

bronze.display: A 230 V mains appliance has a power rating of 920 W. Calculate the current it draws.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange P = VI to I = P/V = 920/230 = 4 A.
I = P ÷ V = 920 ÷ 230 = 4 A. Don't multiply P × V.

bronze.display: A charge of 60 C flows through a component with a voltage of 5 V across it. Calculate the energy transferred.

misconceptions.message: E = QV = 60 × 5 = 300 J. Multiply charge by voltage.

bronze.display: A 2 kW heater is used for 3 hours. Calculate the energy used in kWh.

misconceptions.message: Power is already in kW and time in hours, so just multiply: 2 × 3 = 6 kWh.

bronze.display: A motor transfers 12,000 J of energy in 40 seconds. Calculate its power.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange E = Pt to P = E/t = 12,000/40 = 300 W.
P = E ÷ t = 12,000 ÷ 40 = 300 W. Don't multiply E × t.

bronze.display: Which equation would you use to find the power of a device if you know the current through it and its resistance?

misconceptions.message: With current and resistance, use P = I²R. You'd need P = VI only if you knew the voltage.

silver.display: A 3 kW immersion heater is used for 2 hours. Electricity costs 28p per kWh. Calculate the cost of heating the water in pence.

misconceptions.message: Energy = 3 × 2 = 6 kWh. Cost = 6 × 28 = 168p.
Power must be in kW and time in hours for kWh. 3 kW × 2 h = 6 kWh. Then 6 × 28 = 168p.

silver.display: A microwave has a power rating of 800 W and operates on a 230 V supply. The available fuse ratings are 3 A, 5 A and 13 A. Which fuse should be fitted?

misconceptions.message: I = P/V = 800/230 = 3.48 A. The fuse must be above normal current but as close as possible. 5 A is the correct choice. A 3 A fuse would blow; 13 A is too high to protect the device.

silver.display: A 500 W washing machine runs for 45 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Convert minutes to seconds (× 60), calculate in joules, then convert to kJ (÷ 1000).

silver.display: A 60 W laptop is used for 8 hours a day for 30 days. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. Calculate the total cost in pounds.

misconceptions.message: Convert power: 60 W = 0.06 kW. Total time = 8 × 30 = 240 hours. Energy = 0.06 × 240 = 14.4 kWh. Cost = 14.4 × 30 = 432p = £4.32.
Convert watts to kilowatts first (÷ 1000), then multiply by total hours across all 30 days.

silver.display: A current of 3 A flows through a 15 Ω heating element. Calculate the energy transferred in 2 minutes.

misconceptions.message: First find power: P = I²R = 3² × 15 = 9 × 15 = 135 W. Convert time: 2 min = 120 s. Energy = Pt = 135 × 120 = 16,200 J.
Square the current: 3² = 9, not 3. P = 9 × 15 = 135 W.

silver.display: A 230 V kettle draws 12 A and takes 3 minutes to boil. Calculate the energy transferred to the water in kJ.

misconceptions.message: Convert 3 minutes to 180 seconds before calculating energy. Then convert J to kJ (÷ 1000).

gold.display: Two appliances are used in a house: a 2 kW heater for 5 hours and a 800 W TV for 3 hours. Electricity costs 32p per kWh. Calculate the total cost in pounds.

misconceptions.message: Heater: 2 × 5 = 10 kWh. TV: 0.8 × 3 = 2.4 kWh. Total = 12.4 kWh. Cost = 12.4 × 32 = 396.8p = £3.97 (to nearest penny).
Convert 800 W to 0.8 kW. Don't forget to add both energy values before calculating cost.

gold.display: A kettle is rated at 2.8 kW and is 92% efficient. It transfers 336,000 J of useful energy to the water. Calculate how long the kettle was on for, in seconds.

misconceptions.message: Total input energy = useful ÷ efficiency = 336,000 ÷ 0.92 ≈ 365,217 J. Convert power: 2.8 kW = 2800 W. Time = E/P = 365,217 ÷ 2800 ≈ 130.4 s.
The 336,000 J is useful output, not total input. Divide by efficiency first to get total energy, then find time.

gold.display: An electric shower has a heating element with a resistance of 9.2 Ω and draws a current of 10 A. Calculate the power of the shower.

misconceptions.message: P = I²R = 10² × 9.2 = 100 × 9.2 = 920 W. Remember to square the current.
You have I and R, so use P = I²R. Don't try to use P = VI — you don't know V.

gold.display: A student wants to compare the running cost of two devices over 30 days. Device A: 150 W, used 6 hours/day. Device B: 2 kW, used 30 minutes/day. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. Calculate the difference in cost between the two devices in pounds.

misconceptions.message: Convert 150 W to 0.15 kW and 30 minutes to 0.5 hours. Then calculate kWh for each.

gold.display: A 230 V iron has a power rating of 2300 W. It is used for 20 minutes. Calculate the total charge that flows through the iron.

misconceptions.message: First find current: I = P/V = 2300/230 = 10 A. Convert time: 20 min = 1200 s. Then Q = It = 10 × 1200 = 12,000 C.
Convert 20 minutes to 1200 seconds before using Q = It.
You need two equations here: P = VI to find current, then Q = It to find charge.

gold.display: A 40 W LED TV and a 150 W plasma TV are both used for 5 hours a day. Calculate how much more the plasma TV costs to run per year (365 days) than the LED TV. Electricity costs 30p per kWh. Give your answer in pounds.

misconceptions.message: Convert W to kW: 40 W = 0.04 kW, 150 W = 0.15 kW. Multiply by hours per day × days per year for total kWh.

title: Density, SHC and Latent Heat
description: Calculate density (recall), specific heat capacity and latent heat (both given on the equation sheet) — including multi-step heating-through-state-change problems.

method_card.title: Density, SHC and Latent Heat
method_card.content:
This lesson covers three equations. Density is a recall equation — you must memorise it. SHC and latent heat are given on the equation sheet.

Key strategy — is the temperature changing or is the state changing?

  • If the temperature is going up or down → use specific heat capacity
  • If ice is melting, water is boiling, or any state change is happening → use latent heat
  • If a substance heats up AND changes state, you need two separate calculations added together

Common pitfalls:

  • Always convert grams to kilograms before substituting (÷ 1000)
  • For density, watch the volume units — cm³ and m³ give different density units (g/cm³ vs kg/m³)
  • Temperature change means final minus initial — not just the final temperature
  • During a state change, temperature stays constant — don't add a temperature change for that part
  • Latent heat of fusion (melting) and vaporisation (boiling) are very different values — read the question carefully
steps: Read the question — is the temperature changing or is the state changing (or both)?
Pick the correct equation: density, SHC, or latent heat
Convert units: g → kg, cm³ → m³ if needed, find the temperature change (not just final temp)
Substitute values and calculate
If heating through a state change, do separate SHC + latent heat calculations and add them

exam_context.frequency: High — SHC and latent heat appear most years, density is common on Paper 1 and in required practicals

worked_examples.question: A metal block has a mass of 2.7 kg and a volume of 0.001 m³. Calculate its density.
A 500 g copper block is heated from 20°C to 80°C. The SHC of copper is 385 J/(kg°C). Calculate the energy transferred.
Calculate the total energy needed to heat 0.2 kg of ice at 0°C to steam at 100°C. SHC of water = 4200 J/(kg°C), Lf = 334,000 J/kg, Lv = 2,260,000 J/kg.

steps.label: Step 1 — Melt the ice (latent heat of fusion)
Step 2 — Heat the water from 0°C to 100°C (SHC)
Step 3 — Boil the water (latent heat of vaporisation)

bronze.display: An iron block has a mass of 3.9 kg and a volume of 0.0005 m³. Calculate its density.

misconceptions.message: Density = mass ÷ volume, not volume ÷ mass. ρ = 3.9 ÷ 0.0005 = 7800 kg/m³.

bronze.display: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³ and occupies a volume of 0.002 m³. Calculate its mass.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange ρ = m/V to get m = ρ × V = 800 × 0.002 = 1.6 kg.

bronze.display: A 2 kg block of aluminium is heated from 25°C to 75°C. The SHC of aluminium is 900 J/(kg°C). Calculate the energy transferred.
bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

misconceptions.message: Use the temperature change, not the final temperature. Δθ = 75 − 25 = 50°C. ΔE = 2 × 900 × 50 = 90,000 J.

bronze.display: A 3 kg block of water is heated. The SHC of water is 4200 J/(kg°C). The temperature rises from 20°C to 100°C. Calculate the energy supplied.
bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

bronze.display: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334,000 J/kg.

misconceptions.message: E = m × L = 0.5 × 334,000 = 167,000 J. Don't divide — multiply mass by the specific latent heat.

bronze.display: Calculate the energy needed to boil 0.1 kg of water at 100°C. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2,260,000 J/kg.

misconceptions.message: This is a state change (boiling), so use E = mL. E = 0.1 × 2,260,000 = 226,000 J. Don't use SHC — the temperature isn't changing during boiling.

bronze.display: Which equation would you use to calculate the energy needed to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature?

misconceptions.message: State changes (melting, boiling) use latent heat: E = mL. SHC (mcΔθ) is for temperature changes, not state changes.

bronze.display: A stone has a mass of 0.15 kg and a volume of 0.00005 m³. Calculate its density.

misconceptions.message: ρ = m ÷ V = 0.15 ÷ 0.00005 = 3000 kg/m³. Divide mass by volume, not the other way round.

silver.display: A 400 g piece of copper is heated from 18°C to 118°C. The SHC of copper is 385 J/(kg°C). Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.
silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

misconceptions.message: Find the temperature change first: Δθ = 118 − 18 = 100°C, not 118°C.

silver.display: A heater supplies 50,400 J to 2 kg of water. The SHC of water is 4200 J/(kg°C). Calculate the temperature rise.
silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

silver.display: A gold ring has a density of 19,300 kg/m³ and a mass of 9.65 g. Calculate its volume in cm³. (1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³)

misconceptions.message: Rearrange ρ = m/V to V = m/ρ. Don't multiply mass by density.

silver.display: An immersion heater provides 836,000 J to heat 2.5 kg of water. The SHC of water is 4200 J/(kg°C). The starting temperature is 15°C. Calculate the final temperature.
silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

misconceptions.message: You found the temperature rise (79.6°C), but the question asks for the final temperature. Add the starting temperature: 15 + 79.6 = 94.6°C.

silver.display: Calculate the energy needed to melt 250 g of ice at 0°C. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334,000 J/kg.

misconceptions.message: Convert g to kg first: 250 g = 0.25 kg. E = mL = 0.25 × 334,000 = 83,500 J.

silver.display: A metal block of volume 60 cm³ has a mass of 162 g. Calculate its density in g/cm³.

misconceptions.message: The question asks for g/cm³, so keep the units as given: ρ = 162 ÷ 60 = 2.7 g/cm³. Don't convert to kg and m³.
Density = mass ÷ volume = 162 ÷ 60 = 2.7 g/cm³.

gold.display: Calculate the total energy needed to heat 0.3 kg of ice at 0°C to water at 40°C. SHC of water = 4200 J/(kg°C), specific latent heat of fusion of water = 334,000 J/kg.

misconceptions.message: Two steps needed. Step 1 — melt the ice: E₁ = mL = 0.3 × 334,000 = 100,200 J. Step 2 — heat the water: E₂ = mcΔθ = 0.3 × 4200 × 40 = 50,400 J. Total = 100,200 + 50,400 = 150,600 J.
Melting uses latent heat (E = mL), heating uses SHC (ΔE = mcΔθ). You need both — add them together.

gold.display: Calculate the total energy needed to heat 0.5 kg of water from 20°C to 100°C and then completely boil it. SHC of water = 4200 J/(kg°C), specific latent heat of vaporisation = 2,260,000 J/kg.
A 50 W heater is used to melt 0.5 kg of wax. It takes 8 minutes and 20 seconds to fully melt the wax. Calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of the wax.

misconceptions.message: Convert time: 8 min 20 s = 500 s. Energy = Pt = 50 × 500 = 25,000 J. Then L = E/m = 25,000 ÷ 0.5 = 50,000 J/kg.
From E = mL, rearrange to L = E ÷ m. First find E = Pt = 50 × 500 = 25,000 J. Then L = 25,000 ÷ 0.5 = 50,000 J/kg.

gold.display: An object of mass 120 g is placed in a measuring cylinder containing 50 cm³ of water. The water level rises to 80 cm³. Calculate the density of the object in kg/m³. (1 cm³ = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m³)

misconceptions.message: The volume of the object is the rise in water level: 80 − 50 = 30 cm³, not 80 cm³.

gold.display: A 40 W heater heats 0.8 kg of liquid from 20°C to 30°C in 2 minutes. Calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid.

misconceptions.message: Convert time: 2 min = 120 s. Energy supplied = Pt = 40 × 120 = 4800 J. Δθ = 30 − 20 = 10°C. Rearrange ΔE = mcΔθ → c = ΔE/(mΔθ) = 4800 ÷ (0.8 × 10) = 4800 ÷ 8 = 600 J/(kg°C).
Rearrange ΔE = mcΔθ to c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). Don't multiply all three together.

gold.display: An ice cube of mass 0.05 kg at 0°C is dropped into 0.3 kg of water at 25°C. The ice melts and the final temperature of the water is 21°C. Use this data to estimate the specific latent heat of fusion of ice. SHC of water = 4200 J/(kg°C).

misconceptions.message: Energy lost by warm water = mcΔθ = 0.3 × 4200 × 4 = 5040 J. Energy gained by ice = melting + warming = 0.05L + 0.05 × 4200 × 21 = 0.05L + 4410. Set equal: 5040 = 0.05L + 4410. 0.05L = 630. L = 12,600 J/kg.
Energy lost by warm water = energy gained by ice (melting + warming). Set up: 0.3 × 4200 × 4 = 0.05 × L + 0.05 × 4200 × 21. Solve for L = 12,600 J/kg.

title: Forces, Work Done and Elasticity
description: Calculate weight, work done, spring force (all recall) and elastic potential energy (given on the equation sheet).

method_card.title: Forces, Work Done and Elasticity
method_card.content:
This lesson covers three recall equations (weight, work done, Hooke's law) and one given equation (elastic potential energy, on the sheet).

Key strategy:

  • Weight — mass × gravitational field strength. This often feeds into work done calculations (find weight first, then use it as the force)
  • Work done — force × distance in the direction of the force. Units are joules (same as energy)
  • Hooke's law — force is proportional to extension, but only up to the limit of proportionality
  • Extension — this is not the total length. Extension = stretched length − original (natural) length

Common pitfalls:

  • Work done lifting = weight × height, not mass × height
  • Extension must be in metres (convert cm → m by ÷ 100)
  • Elastic PE has extension squared — doubling the extension quadruples the energy stored
  • Spring constant units are N/m, not N/cm — convert the extension first
  • If a question says "the spring stretches from 12 cm to 20 cm", the extension is 8 cm, not 20 cm
steps: Read the question — are you finding weight, work done, spring force, or elastic energy?
If lifting something, find the weight first (W = mg), then use it in W = Fs
For springs, find the extension (stretched length − natural length) and convert to metres
Substitute into the correct equation and calculate
State your answer with the correct unit (N, J, N/m)

exam_context.frequency: Very high — weight and work done appear almost every year, springs link to required practicals

worked_examples.question: A bag of sugar has a mass of 2 kg. Calculate its weight on Earth. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A person of mass 70 kg climbs a 5 m ladder. Calculate the work done against gravity. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A spring has a spring constant of 40 N/m. It is stretched by 15 cm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.

steps.label: Step 2 — Use elastic PE equation (given on sheet)

bronze.display: A book has a mass of 1.5 kg. Calculate its weight. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Weight = mass × g = 1.5 × 9.8 = 14.7 N. Weight is a force, measured in newtons.

bronze.display: A force of 200 N is used to push a box 6 m along the floor. Calculate the work done.

misconceptions.message: Work done = force × distance = 200 × 6 = 1200 J.

bronze.display: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m and is extended by 0.2 m. Calculate the force on the spring.

misconceptions.message: F = k × e = 25 × 0.2 = 5 N. Multiply spring constant by extension.

bronze.display: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg. Calculate their weight on the Moon, where g = 1.6 N/kg.

misconceptions.message: Use the Moon's g value: W = 80 × 1.6 = 128 N. Don't use Earth's g = 9.8.

bronze.display: A dog pulls a sled with a force of 150 N over a distance of 20 m. Calculate the work done.

misconceptions.message: Work done = F × s = 150 × 20 = 3000 J.

bronze.display: A spring has a natural length of 10 cm. When a 4 N force is applied, it stretches to 18 cm. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.

misconceptions.message: Extension = 18 − 10 = 8 cm = 0.08 m. k = F/e = 4 ÷ 0.08 = 50 N/m. You must convert cm to m first.
Extension is the change in length, not the total length: 18 − 10 = 8 cm.

bronze.display: Which equation gives the weight of an object?

misconceptions.message: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg). W = Fs is work done, not weight — they use the same letter W but mean different things.

bronze.display: A weightlifter raises a 60 kg barbell. Calculate the weight of the barbell. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Weight = mass × g = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N. Weight is measured in newtons, mass in kilograms.

silver.display: A crate of mass 25 kg is lifted 3 m onto a shelf. Calculate the work done against gravity. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: First find the weight: W = mg = 25 × 9.8 = 245 N. Then work done = Fs = 245 × 3 = 735 J. Don't use mass directly in W = Fs.

silver.display: A spring has a spring constant of 80 N/m. It is stretched from its natural length of 12 cm to 27 cm. Calculate the force applied.

misconceptions.message: Use the extension (27 − 12 = 15 cm), not the total stretched length.

silver.display: A forklift lifts a 200 kg pallet 4 m in 10 seconds. Calculate the power of the forklift. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A spring has a spring constant of 60 N/m and is stretched by 0.25 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored. (Equation given on the sheet.)

misconceptions.message: Square the extension: 0.25² = 0.0625. Eₑ = ½ × 60 × 0.0625 = 1.875 J. Don't forget to square e.
Don't forget the ½. Eₑ = ½ × 60 × 0.0625 = 1.875 J, not 3.75 J.

silver.display: A friction force of 500 N acts on a car as it moves 80 m. Calculate the work done against friction in kJ.
A spring is stretched by adding masses. With a 3 N load, the extension is 6 cm. With a 5 N load, the extension is 10 cm. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.

misconceptions.message: Use either data point. 6 cm = 0.06 m. k = F/e = 3 ÷ 0.06 = 50 N/m. (Check: 5 ÷ 0.10 = 50 N/m ✓)
Convert cm to m before dividing. 6 cm = 0.06 m, not 6.

gold.display: A person of mass 65 kg walks up 12 m of stairs in 15 seconds. Calculate the power they develop. (g = 9.8 N/kg)
A spring has a spring constant of 200 N/m. It is stretched from its natural length of 8 cm to 20 cm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.

misconceptions.message: Square the extension: 0.12² = 0.0144. Then Eₑ = ½ × 200 × 0.0144 = 1.44 J.

gold.display: A spring stores 0.72 J of elastic PE when extended by 0.06 m. Calculate the spring constant.

misconceptions.message: Remember e is squared: 0.06² = 0.0036, not 0.06.

gold.display: A box of mass 40 kg is pushed 5 m across a rough floor by a force of 300 N. The friction force is 120 N. Calculate the resultant work done on the box.

misconceptions.message: Resultant force = 300 − 120 = 180 N. Work done = 180 × 5 = 900 J. Subtract friction from the applied force first.
Use the resultant force, not just the applied force. Resultant = 300 − 120 = 180 N. W = 180 × 5 = 900 J.

gold.display: A spring with spring constant 50 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m. The stored energy is transferred to a 0.02 kg ball. Assuming all elastic PE converts to kinetic energy, calculate the speed of the ball.

misconceptions.message: Square the compression: 0.1² = 0.01. Eₑ = ½ × 50 × 0.01 = 0.25 J.

gold.display: A crane lifts a 350 kg beam 8 m and also moves it 15 m horizontally. Calculate the total work done by the crane against gravity. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Work done against gravity only depends on the vertical distance. Weight = 350 × 9.8 = 3430 N. Work done = 3430 × 8 = 27,440 J. The horizontal distance is irrelevant — gravity acts vertically.
Don't add the horizontal distance. Gravity is a vertical force, so only the vertical height matters: W = 3430 × 8 = 27,440 J.

title: Speed, Acceleration and Graphs
description: Calculate speed, acceleration and use distance-time and velocity-time graphs — including the higher-only SUVAT equation v² = u² + 2as.

method_card.title: Speed, Acceleration and Graphs
method_card.content:
This lesson covers two recall equations (speed and acceleration) and one higher-only given equation (the SUVAT equation on the sheet).

Key strategy for graphs:

  • Distance-time graph: the gradient (slope) gives the speed. A steeper line = faster. A flat line = stationary. A curve = changing speed (accelerating or decelerating)
  • Velocity-time graph: the gradient gives the acceleration. The area under the graph gives the total distance travelled

Common pitfalls:

  • Speed = distance ÷ time, not time ÷ distance
  • Acceleration uses change in velocity (final − initial), not just the final speed
  • Convert units carefully: km/h to m/s → divide by 3.6
  • Area under a v-t graph can be split into rectangles and triangles
  • Deceleration is just negative acceleration — the object is slowing down
  • The higher-tier equation has v squared — don't forget to square root at the end
steps: Read the question — speed, acceleration, or graph interpretation?
For graphs: gradient = speed (d-t) or acceleration (v-t); area under v-t graph = distance
Convert units if needed (km to m, hours to seconds, km/h to m/s)
Substitute into the correct equation and calculate
Check: is the answer reasonable? (A person walks ~1.5 m/s, runs ~8 m/s, cars ~30 m/s)

exam_context.frequency: Very high — motion graphs and calculations appear on almost every Paper 1

worked_examples.question: A car travels 240 m in 8 seconds. Calculate its speed.
A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels during this time using the velocity-time graph method.

steps.label: Step 1 — Area under v-t graph = distance
steps.content: The v-t graph forms a trapezium from 10 m/s to 25 m/s over 6 s.

worked_examples.question: A car accelerates from rest at 2 m/s². Calculate its speed after travelling 100 m. (Use v² = u² + 2as)

steps.label: Step 1 — Identify SUVAT values
steps.content: u = 0 m/s (from rest), a = 2 m/s², s = 100 m, v = ?

bronze.display: A cyclist travels 600 m in 40 seconds. Calculate their speed.

misconceptions.message: Speed = distance ÷ time = 600 ÷ 40 = 15 m/s. Don't divide time by distance.

bronze.display: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 10 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

misconceptions.message: Change in velocity = 25 − 5 = 20 m/s. Acceleration = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s².

bronze.display: A runner moves at a constant speed of 4 m/s for 30 seconds. Calculate the distance covered.

misconceptions.message: Distance = speed × time = 4 × 30 = 120 m.

bronze.display: A train decelerates from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate the deceleration.

misconceptions.message: Δv = 10 − 30 = −20 m/s. a = −20 ÷ 5 = −4 m/s². The deceleration is 4 m/s² (magnitude).

bronze.display: The distance-time graph shows a journey. Calculate the speed during the first 15 seconds.
bronze.equation_hint: Gradient of a distance-time graph = speed

misconceptions.message: Speed = gradient = rise ÷ run = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 m/s. The graph is straight from 0 to 15 s, showing constant speed.

bronze.display: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s. How far does it travel in 0.5 seconds?

misconceptions.message: Distance = speed × time = 340 × 0.5 = 170 m.

bronze.display: A bus accelerates from rest to 12 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

misconceptions.message: From rest means u = 0. a = (12 − 0) ÷ 6 = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m/s².

bronze.display: How long does it take a car travelling at 20 m/s to cover 500 m?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange s = vt → t = s/v = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 s.

silver.display: A car travels 54 km in 30 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s.
A car travelling at 108 km/h brakes and stops in 5 seconds. Calculate the deceleration in m/s².

misconceptions.message: Convert: 108 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s. Δv = 0 − 30 = −30 m/s. a = −30 ÷ 5 = −6 m/s². Deceleration = 6 m/s².
Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. 108 ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s.

silver.display: The velocity-time graph shows a car's journey. Calculate the total distance travelled in 20 seconds.
silver.equation_hint: Area under a velocity-time graph = distance

misconceptions.message: Area under a v-t graph = distance. Split into: triangle (0–10 s) = ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m, rectangle (10–20 s) = 10 × 20 = 200 m. Total = 100 + 200 = 300 m.
Split the area: 0–10 s is a triangle (½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m). 10–20 s is a rectangle (10 × 20 = 200 m). Total = 300 m.

silver.display: A car accelerates uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels. (Hint: average speed × time)

misconceptions.message: Average speed = (8 + 20) ÷ 2 = 14 m/s. Distance = 14 × 4 = 56 m.

silver.display: A sprinter accelerates at 4 m/s² from rest. Calculate their speed after 3 seconds, and the distance covered.
silver.equation_hint: \(v = u + at\) and average speed \(= \frac{u + v}{2}\)

misconceptions.message: v = u + at = 0 + 4 × 3 = 12 m/s. Average speed = (0 + 12) ÷ 2 = 6 m/s. Distance = 6 × 3 = 18 m. The question asks for the distance.

silver.display: A car travels at 90 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
silver.equation_hint: Divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s

misconceptions.message: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 m/s. To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6 (or multiply by 1000 and divide by 3600).

gold.display: A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s². Calculate its velocity after travelling 150 m.

misconceptions.message: The equation gives v², so you must square root: v = √900 = 30 m/s, not 900 m/s.

gold.display: A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 4 m/s². Calculate the braking distance.

misconceptions.message: Deceleration means a is negative: a = −4 m/s². The car stops, so v = 0.

gold.display: The velocity-time graph shows a complete journey. Calculate the total distance travelled.

misconceptions.message: Split into 3 sections. 0–6 s: triangle = ½ × 6 × 15 = 45 m. 6–8 s: rectangle = 2 × 15 = 30 m. 8–14 s: triangle = ½ × 6 × 15 = 45 m. Total = 45 + 30 + 45 = 120 m.
Find the area under the graph — not the gradient. Split into triangles and rectangles.

gold.display: A stone is dropped from rest and hits the ground at 24.5 m/s. Calculate the height it fell from. Use \(g = 9.8\) m/s².

A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 15 m/s. It accelerates over 100 m to reach a new speed. The resultant force on the car is 3600 N. Calculate the final speed of the car. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

misconceptions.message: First find acceleration: a = F/m = 3600 ÷ 1200 = 3 m/s². Then use v² = u² + 2as = 15² + 2 × 3 × 100 = 225 + 600 = 825. v = √825 = 28.7 m/s.
You need two equations here: F = ma gives a = 3 m/s², then v² = u² + 2as gives the final speed.

gold.display: A cyclist accelerates from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 seconds, then travels at a constant 10 m/s for another 7 seconds. Calculate the total distance covered in 10 seconds.

misconceptions.message: Two phases. Accelerating (0–3 s): average speed = (4 + 10)/2 = 7 m/s, distance = 7 × 3 = 21 m. Constant speed (3–10 s): distance = 10 × 7 = 70 m. Total = 21 + 70 = 91 m.
During acceleration, use the average speed (not just 10 m/s). Average = (4 + 10)/2 = 7 m/s.

title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Waves
description: Calculate resultant force and acceleration (F = ma), momentum (HT only), wave speed and period — with standard form for wave calculations.

method_card.title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Waves
method_card.content:
This lesson covers three recall equations (Newton's second law, momentum, wave speed) and one given equation (period, on the sheet). Momentum is higher tier only.

Key strategy for F = ma:

  • Always use the resultant force — if there's friction or drag, subtract it from the driving force before using F = ma
  • If an object moves at constant velocity, the resultant force is zero (forces are balanced)

Key strategy for waves:

  • Convert units carefully: kHz → Hz (× 1000), MHz → Hz (× 1,000,000), cm → m (÷ 100)
  • Period and frequency are reciprocals: if you know one, flip it to get the other
  • Speed of light/EM waves = 3 × 10⁸ m/s — use this unless told otherwise

Common pitfalls:

  • Mass must be in kg, not grams. 500 g = 0.5 kg
  • In momentum conservation, total momentum before = total momentum after. Watch the direction — objects moving in opposite directions have opposite signs
  • Don't confuse wave speed with speed of sound (340 m/s) and speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m/s)
steps: Read the question — is it force/acceleration, momentum, wave speed, or period?
For F = ma: find the resultant force first (subtract opposing forces from driving force)
For waves: convert all units (kHz → Hz, cm → m) before substituting
Substitute and calculate — for momentum conservation, set total p before = total p after
State your answer with the correct unit and in standard form if the numbers are very large or small

exam_context.frequency: Very high — F = ma and wave calculations appear almost every year. Momentum is HT only but frequently tested

worked_examples.question: A resultant force of 600 N acts on a 50 kg object. Calculate its acceleration.
A car has a driving force of 4000 N and friction of 1200 N. Its mass is 1400 kg. Calculate its acceleration.
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together. Calculate the velocity after the collision.

steps.label: Step 1 — Momentum before
steps.content: p = mv. Trolley A: 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s. Trolley B: 1 × 0 = 0. Total = 6 kg m/s

bronze.display: A resultant force of 240 N acts on an 80 kg trolley. Calculate its acceleration.

misconceptions.message: a = F ÷ m = 240 ÷ 80 = 3 m/s². Don't multiply F × m.

bronze.display: Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 1500 kg car at 2 m/s².

misconceptions.message: F = ma = 1500 × 2 = 3000 N. No rearranging needed here.

bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Calculate its speed.

misconceptions.message: v = f × λ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m/s. Multiply frequency by wavelength.

bronze.display: A water wave has a speed of 2 m/s and a wavelength of 0.5 m. Calculate its frequency.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange v = fλ → f = v/λ = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 Hz.

bronze.display: A 10 N force accelerates a 2 kg object. Calculate the acceleration.
A wave has a frequency of 200 Hz. Calculate its period.

misconceptions.message: T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 200 = 0.005 s. Period and frequency are reciprocals.

bronze.display: Which equation links force, mass and acceleration?

misconceptions.message: Newton's second law: F = ma. p = mv is momentum, v = fλ is wave speed, W = mg is weight.

bronze.display: A wave has a speed of 330 m/s and a frequency of 660 Hz. Calculate the wavelength.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange v = fλ → λ = v/f = 330 ÷ 660 = 0.5 m.

silver.display: A car has a driving force of 3500 N and a friction force of 500 N. Its mass is 1200 kg. Calculate its acceleration.

misconceptions.message: Find the resultant force first: 3500 − 500 = 3000 N. Then a = F/m = 3000 ÷ 1200 = 2.5 m/s².
Use the resultant force (3500 − 500 = 3000 N), not the driving force alone.

silver.display: A sound wave has a frequency of 2 kHz and a wavelength of 17 cm. Calculate the speed of sound.

misconceptions.message: Convert units: 2 kHz = 2000 Hz, 17 cm = 0.17 m. v = fλ = 2000 × 0.17 = 340 m/s.

silver.display: A 500 g toy car is pushed with a force of 4 N. Friction is 1.5 N. Calculate its acceleration.

misconceptions.message: Convert: 500 g = 0.5 kg. Resultant force = 4 − 1.5 = 2.5 N. a = 2.5 ÷ 0.5 = 5 m/s².
Subtract friction: resultant = 4 − 1.5 = 2.5 N. Then a = 2.5 ÷ 0.5 = 5 m/s².

silver.display: A moving object of mass 4 kg has a momentum of 20 kg m/s. Calculate its velocity.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange p = mv → v = p/m = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s.

silver.display: A microwave has a frequency of 2.45 GHz. The speed of EM waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the wavelength. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
A wave has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate its frequency, then find the wavelength if the wave speed is 5 m/s.
silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\), then \(v = f\lambda\)

gold.display: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together and move off. Calculate the velocity after the collision.

misconceptions.message: Total momentum before = 3 × 4 + 1 × 0 = 12 kg m/s. After: combined mass = 4 kg. v = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m/s.
Momentum is conserved: total before = total after. 12 = 4v, so v = 3 m/s.

gold.display: A 0.05 kg bullet is fired at 400 m/s into a 2.95 kg block of wood on a frictionless surface. The bullet embeds in the block. Calculate the velocity of the block and bullet after the collision.

misconceptions.message: Momentum before: bullet = 0.05 × 400 = 20 kg m/s, block = 0. Total = 20 kg m/s. After: total mass = 0.05 + 2.95 = 3 kg. v = 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 m/s.
Conservation of momentum: 0.05 × 400 = 3 × v. v = 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 m/s.

gold.display: A rocket of mass 500 kg fires its engines, producing a thrust of 8000 N. Its weight is 4900 N. Calculate the resultant force and the acceleration.

misconceptions.message: Resultant force = thrust − weight = 8000 − 4900 = 3100 N upwards. a = F/m = 3100 ÷ 500 = 6.2 m/s².
Don't forget the weight acts downward. Resultant = 8000 − 4900 = 3100 N. Then a = 3100 ÷ 500 = 6.2 m/s².

gold.display: A radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz. The speed of radio waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the wavelength in standard form.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange v = fλ to λ = v/f. Don't multiply speed by frequency.

gold.display: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates at 2 m/s² for 8 seconds. The driving force is 3200 N. Calculate the friction force acting on the car.

misconceptions.message: Resultant force = ma = 1000 × 2 = 2000 N. Resultant = driving − friction. 2000 = 3200 − friction. Friction = 3200 − 2000 = 1200 N.
First find the resultant force from F = ma, then use: friction = driving force − resultant force.

gold.display: An X-ray has a wavelength of \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. The speed of EM waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the frequency of the X-ray. Give your answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: When dividing powers of 10: 10⁸ ÷ 10⁻¹⁰ = 10⁸⁻⁽⁻¹⁰⁾ = 10¹⁸.
